# Filtering by File Type in ripgrep

When you search with ripgrep, you often find yourself running the same pattern over and over against the same kinds of files. If you're searching only C files one day and only Rust files the next, typing out the glob patterns each time gets tedious. That's where ripgrep's file type system comes in.

## What file types do

A file type is a named bundle of filename patterns (called globs) grouped together so you can reference them by name instead of by pattern. ripgrep comes with about 150 built-in types. Instead of typing:

```
$ rg 'pattern' -g '*.rs'
```

You can write:

```
$ rg 'pattern' --type rust
```

The end result is the same: ripgrep searches only Rust files. But the second command is shorter and less error-prone. You don't have to remember that Rust files end in `.rs`. ripgrep already knows.

Some types encompass multiple file extensions. The C type, for instance, matches both `.c` source files and `.h` header files. If you wanted to do that with globs:

```
$ rg 'int main' -g '*.{c,h}'
```

With types, it's just:

```
$ rg 'int main' --type c
```

## Using `--type` and `--type-not`

The `--type` flag tells ripgrep to search only files of a given type. You can use the long form or the short `-t` abbreviation:

```
$ rg 'function_name' --type python
$ rg 'function_name' -t python
```

You can specify multiple types. ripgrep will search any file matching any of the types you list:

```
$ rg 'TODO' --type python --type rust
```

The `--type-not` flag does the opposite: it excludes files of a given type. Use it with the long form or the short `-T` abbreviation:

```
$ rg 'TODO' --type-not json
$ rg 'TODO' -T json
```

You can also exclude multiple types:

```
$ rg 'TODO' --type-not json --type-not yaml
```

One important detail: the `--type` and `--type-not` flags have lower precedence than glob patterns you specify with `-g/--glob`. This means if you use both together, the glob takes priority. The same applies to patterns in `.gitignore` or `.ignore` files.

## Listing available types

ripgrep comes with many built-in types. To see the full list of available types and the glob patterns each one matches, run:

```
$ rg --type-list
```

This shows output like:

```
c: *.[chH], *.[chH].in, *.cats
cpp: *.C, *.cc, *.cpp, *.cxx, *.h, *.hh, *.hpp, *.hxx
python: *.py
rust: *.rs, *.rs.in
```

Each line shows the type name, a colon, and a comma-separated list of glob patterns that make up that type. You can search this output for the type you're interested in:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg rust
rust: *.rs, *.rs.in
```

## Creating custom types with `--type-add`

The built-in types cover a lot of ground, but sometimes you need a type that isn't predefined. The `--type-add` flag lets you create your own types on the fly. You specify a new type name and one or more glob patterns for it:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -t web 'title'
```

This creates a new type called `web` that matches HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files. The `-t web` flag then uses this type to search for the word `title` only in those files.

You can add multiple globs to a single type in one flag by using glob expansion syntax:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -t web 'title'
```

This does the same thing: creates a `web` type matching all three file extensions, then searches only in those files.

If you want to verify that your new type was added correctly, use `--type-list` together with `--type-add`:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' --type-list | rg web
web: *.html, *.css, *.js
```

A crucial point: `--type-add` only applies to the current ripgrep command. If you close your terminal and run ripgrep again, your custom type is gone. It's not persisted anywhere. If you want a custom type to be available every time you run ripgrep, you have two options.

First, create a shell alias:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

Second, add the `--type-add` flag to a ripgrep configuration file. ripgrep reads configuration from `~/.config/ripgrep/config` (on macOS and Linux) or `%APPDATA%\ripgrep\config` (on Windows). Add one flag per line:

```
--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}
```

Now every ripgrep invocation will include this type definition without you typing it.

## The special `all` type

ripgrep supports a special type name: `all`. When you use `--type all`, ripgrep searches all files whose types are recognized by ripgrep. In other words, it searches only files that match at least one of ripgrep's known types:

```
$ rg 'pattern' --type all
```

This is useful if you want to exclude unrecognized files (like binary files or media). It's equivalent to running `--type` for every single type ripgrep knows about.

The opposite is `--type-not all`, which searches only files that ripgrep doesn't recognize by type:

```
$ rg 'pattern' --type-not all
```

Note that a file without an extension might not match any type. For example, the shell type matches `.bash` and `.sh` files, but not a shell script without an extension. So a bare script file named `my-script` won't match the shell type. That's why `--type-not all` would include it but `--type sh` wouldn't.

## Combining type filters

You can combine `--type` and `--type-not` in the same command:

```
$ rg 'pattern' --type python --type-not test
```

This searches Python files but excludes those with the `test` type. You can use type filters alongside glob patterns for even more control over what files ripgrep searches.

The type system is there to save you typing and to make your searches more reliable by removing the guesswork about filename patterns.
